title: No. 49 — Method of Guarding Against the Encroachments of Any One Department of Government by Appealing to the People Through a Convention. (Madison)
paragraphs: The author of the "Notes on the State of Virginia," whom I quoted in the last paper, attached to that valuable work the draft of a constitution. It had been prepared to be laid before a convention that the legislature was expected to call in 1783 to establish a constitution for that commonwealth. The plan, like everything from the same pen, shows an original, comprehensive and accurate turn of mind. It deserves attention all the more because it displays both a fervent attachment to republican government and an enlightened view of the dangerous tendencies against which such a government ought to be guarded. One of the precautions he proposes, and the one on which he seems finally to rely as a safeguard for the weaker departments of power against invasions by the stronger, is perhaps entirely his own. Since it bears directly on the subject of our present inquiry, it should not be overlooked.

His proposal is "that whenever any two of the three branches of government shall concur in opinion, each by the voices of two thirds of their whole number, that a convention is necessary for altering the constitution, or CORRECTING BREACHES OF IT, a convention shall be called for the purpose."

The people are the only legitimate fountain of power, and the constitutional charter under which the separate branches of government hold their power is derived from them. It therefore seems entirely consistent with republican theory to return to that same original authority, not only whenever the powers of the government need to be enlarged, reduced or remodeled, but also whenever any one of the departments encroaches on the chartered authorities of the others. The separate departments are perfectly co-ordinate under the terms of their common commission. It is evident that none of them can claim an exclusive or superior right to settle the boundaries between their respective powers. How, then, are the encroachments of the stronger to be prevented, or the wrongs of the weaker to be redressed, without an appeal to the people themselves? As the grantors of the commissions, they alone can declare its true meaning and enforce its observance.

There is certainly great force in this reasoning. It must be granted to prove that a constitutional road to the decision of the people ought to be marked out and kept open for certain great and extraordinary occasions. But there appear to be insuperable objections to the proposed recourse to the people as a provision for keeping the separate departments of power within their constitutional limits in all cases.

In the first place, the provision does not reach the case of two of the departments combining against the third. The legislative authority has so many ways of working on the motives of the other departments. Suppose it should win over to its side either of the others, or even one third of the members of either. The remaining department could then derive no benefit from this remedy. I do not dwell on this objection, however, because it may be thought to count against the particular form of the principle rather than against the principle itself.

In the next place, there is an objection that may be considered inherent in the principle. Every appeal to the people would carry an implication that the government has some defect. Frequent appeals would therefore, to a great extent, deprive the government of the veneration that time bestows on everything, and without which even the wisest and freest governments would perhaps lack the stability they require. If it is true that all governments rest on opinion, it is no less true that the strength of opinion in each individual, and its practical influence on his conduct, depend greatly on the number of others he supposes to have held the same opinion. The reason of man, like man himself, is timid and cautious when left alone, and gains firmness and confidence in proportion to the number with which it is associated. When the examples that fortify opinion are ANCIENT as well as NUMEROUS, they are known to have a double effect. In a nation of philosophers this consideration ought to be disregarded, because the voice of enlightened reason would be enough to instill a reverence for the laws. But a nation of philosophers is as little to be expected as the philosophical race of kings that Plato wished for. And in every other nation, even the most rational government will find it no superfluous advantage to have the prejudices of the community on its side.

The danger of disturbing the public tranquillity by stirring the public passions too strongly is a still more serious objection to frequently referring constitutional questions to the decision of the whole society. Our established forms of government have been revised with success, which does much honor to the virtue and intelligence of the people of America. Even so, it must be admitted that such experiments are too delicate to be multiplied without need. We should remember that all the existing constitutions were formed in the midst of a danger that held down the passions most hostile to order and harmony. They were formed amid an enthusiastic confidence of the people in their patriotic leaders, which silenced the ordinary diversity of opinion on great national questions. They were formed amid a universal ardor for new and opposite forms, produced by a universal resentment and indignation against the old government. And they were formed at a time when no spirit of party, connected with the changes to be made or the abuses to be reformed, could mix its leaven into the work. The situations in which we must expect usually to find ourselves in the future offer no equivalent security against the danger that is feared.

But the greatest objection of all is that the decisions likely to result from such appeals would not serve the purpose of maintaining the constitutional equilibrium of the government. We have seen that the tendency of republican governments is for the legislative department to aggrandize itself at the expense of the others. The appeals to the people, therefore, would usually be made by the executive and judiciary departments. But whichever side made them, would each side have equal advantages in the trial? Let us look at their different situations. The members of the executive and judiciary departments are few in number and can be personally known to only a small part of the people. The judges, because of the way they are appointed and the nature and permanence of their tenure, are too far removed from the people to share much in their prepossessions. The executive officers are generally objects of jealousy, and their administration can always be distorted and made unpopular. The members of the legislative department, on the other hand, are numerous. They are scattered among the people at large and live among them. Their ties of blood, friendship and acquaintance reach a great proportion of the most influential part of society. The nature of their public trust implies a personal influence among the people and implies that they are more directly the trusted guardians of the rights and liberties of the people. With these advantages, it can hardly be supposed that the opposing party would have an equal chance of a favorable outcome.

But the legislative party would not only be able to plead its cause most successfully with the people. It would probably also be made the judge. The same influence that had won them election to the legislature would win them a seat in the convention. If this should not hold for all of them, it would probably hold for many, and quite certainly for those leading figures on whom everything depends in such bodies. In short, the convention would be composed chiefly of men who had been, who actually were, or who expected to be members of the department whose conduct was being charged. They would consequently be parties to the very question they were to decide.

It might happen, however, that appeals would sometimes be made under circumstances less unfavorable to the executive and judiciary departments. The usurpations of the legislature might be so flagrant and so sudden as to admit of no plausible disguise. A strong party within the legislature itself might take the side of the other branches. The executive power might be in the hands of a special favorite of the people. In such a state of things, the public decision might be less swayed by prepossessions in favor of the legislative party. But it could still never be expected to turn on the true merits of the question. It would inevitably be bound up with the spirit of already existing parties, or of parties springing out of the question itself. It would be bound up with persons of distinguished character and wide influence in the community. And it would be pronounced by the very men who had been agents in, or opponents of, the measures to which the decision would relate. The PASSIONS of the public, therefore, not its REASON, would sit in judgment. But it is the reason of the public alone that ought to control and regulate the government. The passions ought to be controlled and regulated by the government.

The last paper showed that mere declarations in a written constitution cannot hold the separate departments to their legal rights. This paper has shown that occasional appeals to the people would be neither a fitting nor an effective way to do it. I will not examine how well the other kinds of provision in the plan I quoted might work. Some of them rest, without question, on sound political principles, and all of them are drawn up with unusual ingenuity and precision.
